title: Memory allocation, fragmentation, swap, OOM killer, mmap, page cache
scopeHtml: Scope: allocators and brk/mmap, fragmentation, swap and zram, overcommit and OOM killer, mmap, page cache and fsync, memory triage.

notes.title: How programs get memory
notes.html:
A program asks for memory in layers: your code calls an allocator (malloc, new, the JVM heap), and the allocator asks the kernel only when it runs out.

Kernel-level calls:

  • brk/sbrk: move the end of the heap segment up or down. Simple, contiguous.
  • mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS): map a fresh zeroed region anywhere; used for big allocations (glibc threshold M_MMAP_THRESHOLD, 128 KB default, dynamic) and for thread arenas.

Neither commits RAM immediately. Physical frames arrive on first touch via page faults (see the virtual memory note).

$ strace -e trace=brk,mmap,munmap ./app
brk(NULL)                                 = 0x55e1c8a3c000
brk(0x55e1c8a5d000)                       = 0x55e1c8a5d000      # heap grew 132 KB
mmap(NULL, 1048576, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0) = 0x7f2c...

Worked example. new byte[100MB] in Java: JVM already reserved the heap at start with mmap; the allocation just advances a pointer, but the first write to each 4 KB page faults (25,600 minor faults). -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch pays that up front.

Industry examples. glibc ptmalloc, Google tcmalloc, Facebook jemalloc (used by Redis, Firefox, Rust earlier) and mimalloc are all user-space allocators layered on mmap/brk. Switching Redis from glibc to jemalloc was done for lower fragmentation. Android uses Scudo (hardened) as its native allocator.

Everyday analogy. A shop (allocator) buys stock from the wholesaler (kernel) in big boxes and hands customers small amounts, only reordering when the shelf is empty.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying malloc = syscall. It is a library function; the syscall occurs only to grow.
  • Believing free always returns memory to the OS. Usually it goes back to the allocator's free list.

notes.title: Allocator internals
notes.html:
An allocator carves big chunks into variable-sized blocks and tracks which are free.

Typical design (glibc-style):

  • Each block has a small header with its size (so free(p) knows how much to release).
  • Free blocks are kept in bins by size class: small exact-size bins, large sorted bins.
  • Freed neighbours are coalesced into bigger blocks.
  • Thread caches/arenas (tcache in glibc, per-thread caches in tcmalloc/jemalloc) avoid taking a global lock on every allocation: key for multicore speed.

Placement policies (textbook): first fit, next fit, best fit, worst fit. Real allocators use size classes (powers of two-ish) which is segregated-fit: fast O(1) allocation at the cost of some internal waste.

[hdr|used 32][hdr|FREE 64][hdr|used 16][hdr|FREE 128]
         free(2nd) next to free neighbour -> coalesce into one bigger FREE block

Allocator choice in production: jemalloc and tcmalloc usually lower fragmentation and contention than glibc for long-running, multi-threaded servers. Switching is easy and reversible, often with LD_PRELOAD=libjemalloc.so.

MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 ./app      # limit glibc per-thread arenas (fixes RSS growth in many-thread apps)
LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/libjemalloc.so.2 ./app

Production incident. A Java or native service's RSS creeps up for days with a stable heap: glibc created up to 8 x cores arenas, each retaining freed memory. Setting MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 or using jemalloc fixes it. Metric: container working set rising while app-level heap is flat.

Everyday analogy. A parking lot where each car (allocation) has a size; when cars leave, neighbouring empty spots merge into a larger one for a truck.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing JVM heap management (garbage collector) with the native allocator underneath.
  • Forgetting per-thread caches trade memory for speed.

notes.title: Fragmentation
notes.html:
Fragmentation is memory that is free but unusable.

  • Internal: waste inside an allocated block. Ask for 33 bytes, allocator gives a 48-byte class. A 4 KB page serving a 100-byte object wastes 3,996 bytes.
  • External: plenty of total free memory but split into small holes, so a large request fails. 100 MB free in 1 MB pieces cannot satisfy a 10 MB request.

Paging eliminates external fragmentation of RAM for ordinary allocations (any frame fits any page) but it returns for things that need physically contiguous memory (huge pages, DMA buffers, kernel allocations). Linux counters this with the buddy allocator (power-of-two blocks, merges buddies on free), the slab/SLUB allocator for small kernel objects, and compaction (kcompactd). Look at it:

$ cat /proc/buddyinfo
Node 0, zone Normal  3410 2210  980  240  41  2  0  0  0  0  0
#                      4K   8K  16K  32K ... 4M   <- zero big blocks: fragmented
$ cat /proc/slabinfo | head      # or slabtop

User-space fragmentation: long-running processes with mixed object lifetimes leave holes; RSS stays high though live data is small. Redis reports mem_fragmentation_ratio (RSS / used memory); above 1.5 means significant waste; activedefrag yes helps. Java copying/compacting collectors (G1, ZGC) move objects to defragment.

Worked example. Redis holds 10 GB of live data; INFO memory shows used_memory_rss 16 GB, ratio 1.6. Six GB of RAM is lost. Options: enable active defrag, restart a replica and fail over (a standard trick), use jemalloc.

Everyday analogy. A bookshelf with many one-book gaps: lots of free room in total, but no gap fits an encyclopaedia set.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying paging has no fragmentation at all (internal fragmentation of the last page, and contiguous-memory needs).
  • Treating a high Redis fragmentation ratio below 1 as good: under 1 means it is swapped.

notes.title: Swap
notes.html:
Swap is disk space (a partition or file) used to hold anonymous memory pages evicted from RAM. File-backed clean pages never need swap; they are simply dropped and re-read.

Why have swap: it lets the kernel push cold, never-touched pages (idle daemon heap) out so RAM serves the hot working set and page cache; it gives a buffer against sudden spikes. Why avoid it for latency-critical services: a swapped-in page is a major fault costing 0.1 to 10 ms, and a swapping JVM stalls GC badly.

Tuning:

  • vm.swappiness (default 60): how readily to swap anonymous pages vs drop cache. Databases commonly use 1 to 10. It is a preference, not an on/off.
  • zram/zswap: compress pages in RAM first (2x to 3x ratio), the default on many laptops and Android phones. Android swaps to zram, never to flash widely, to protect flash wear.
  • Kubernetes: swap was disallowed by default for years; newer versions support limited node swap (confirm for your version).
swapon --show
cat /proc/swaps
vmstat 1          # si (swap in) and so (swap out) KB/s
grep -E 'SwapTotal|SwapFree' /proc/meminfo
for f in /proc/*/status; do awk '/Name|VmSwap/{printf $2" "}END{print ""}' $f; done | sort -k2 -n | tail   # who is swapped

Worked example. A 16 GB server running a 10 GB database plus 8 GB of cold daemons: with 4 GB swap, the kernel parks 3 GB of cold heap, leaving the DB's cache intact. Without swap, the DB's buffer cache shrinks first. Sustained si/so above a few MB/s, though, means a real shortage.

Everyday analogy. Storing winter clothes in the loft: fine for stuff you rarely need, painful if you must climb up every morning.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "swap off is always best".
  • Believing swap usage alone proves a problem. Active swap traffic (si/so) is the signal, not the used amount.

notes.title: Overcommit and the OOM killer
notes.html:
Linux by default lets processes allocate more virtual memory than exists (overcommit), betting that most will never touch it all. If the bet fails, the OOM killer picks a process and kills it with SIGKILL.

Controls:

  • vm.overcommit_memory: 0 heuristic (default, refuses only obviously absurd requests), 1 always allow (Redis recommends for fork), 2 strict (limit = swap + ratio x RAM; allocations fail up front).
  • OOM selection: each process gets oom_score (roughly its share of memory, adjusted); the highest is killed. Tweak with /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj (-1000 never kill, +1000 kill first). Kubelet/systemd set these (Guaranteed pods are protected, BestEffort die first).
  • cgroup OOM: a container with a memory limit (memory.max) gets killed when it hits the limit even if the host has free RAM. Kubernetes shows OOMKilled, exit code 137.

Reading the evidence:

$ dmesg -T | grep -i -A3 'out of memory'
Out of memory: Killed process 4410 (java) total-vm:9123456kB, anon-rss:7654320kB, file-rss:0kB, shmem-rss:0kB, UID:1000 pgtables:15424kB oom_score_adj:0
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<grp>/memory.events
oom 0
oom_kill 2
$ kubectl describe pod x | grep -A3 'Last State'
    Reason: OOMKilled    Exit Code: 137

Typical root causes: a JVM whose -Xmx plus metaspace, thread stacks (1 MB each x 500 threads) and direct buffers exceeds the container limit (set heap to about 60 to 75% of the limit, or -XX:MaxRAMPercentage); unbounded caches or queues; memory leaks; per-connection buffers.

Industry examples. Facebook built oomd (userspace, uses PSI) to kill by policy before the kernel does; Android's lmkd kills background apps to keep the UI responsive; Redis docs warn that fork + overcommit 0 can fail under pressure.

Decision gravity. Strict overcommit (2) makes failures show as clean ENOMEM at allocation but wastes capacity and breaks fork-heavy apps; heuristic overcommit maximises utilisation at the risk of surprise kills. Easy to change at runtime, hard to size correctly.

Everyday analogy. An airline overbooking seats: usually fine, and when everyone turns up, somebody gets bumped.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the OOM killer picks the process that allocated last. It scores by usage.
  • Debugging an OOMKilled pod by looking only at the heap; native memory counts.

notes.title: mmap
notes.html:
mmap maps a file (or anonymous memory) directly into the address space, so you read and write it as ordinary memory and the kernel handles loading.

Flavours:

  • File-backed, MAP_SHARED: writes go to the page cache and later to the file; visible to other mappers. Used for databases and IPC.
  • File-backed, MAP_PRIVATE: copy-on-write; changes are private. How the loader maps executables and libraries.
  • Anonymous: zeroed memory (malloc big blocks, thread stacks, shared memory before fork).

Benefits: no read copy into a user buffer (the page cache page is mapped directly), lazy loading, multiple processes share one cached copy, easy random access. Drawbacks: page faults replace explicit I/O (unpredictable latency, major faults on a cold miss), no clean error handling (an I/O error becomes SIGBUS), TLB shootdown costs on unmap, and writing back is out of the app's control (msync forces it). The CMU "Are you sure you want to use MMAP in your DBMS?" paper led several databases to prefer explicit buffer pools.

import mmap
with open("data.bin", "r+b") as f:
    m = mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0)    # map whole file
    print(m[0:16])                  # reads fault pages in lazily
    m[0:4] = b"ABCD"                # dirties a page, flushed later
    m.flush()                       # msync

Inspect: cat /proc/<pid>/maps lists mappings; pmap -x shows RSS per mapping; large Mapped: in /proc/meminfo.

Worked example. Searching a 50 GB index file with read() needs buffer copies and a cache of your own; with mmap on a 64 GB box the whole file lives once in page cache and 20 processes share it, so total RAM used is 50 GB, not 1 TB.

Industry examples. LMDB, Lucene/Elasticsearch (MMapDirectory), Kafka (index files; log reads use sendfile zero-copy), SQLite optional mmap, Android loading .so/dex via mmap.

Everyday analogy. Pinning a giant map on the wall and reading it by looking, rather than asking an assistant to photocopy sections for you.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing mmap is always faster than read/write. For sequential streaming the difference is small; for random access it helps; page-fault overhead can hurt.
  • Forgetting SIGBUS when the file is truncated under a mapping.

notes.title: Page cache
notes.html:
The page cache is RAM that Linux uses to keep recently read and written file data, so most file I/O never touches the disk. It uses nearly all otherwise free memory and gives it back under pressure. This is why free shows low "free" but high buff/cache.

Behaviour:

  • Read: first read goes to disk and fills the cache (a cache miss, around 100 microseconds on NVMe, ms on HDD); subsequent reads come from RAM (about 100 ns to 1 microsecond with the copy).
  • Readahead: the kernel guesses sequential access and pre-reads ahead (default 128 KB, blockdev --getra).
  • Write-back: writes land in cache as dirty pages; flusher threads write them out after vm.dirty_expire_centisecs (30 s) or when dirty memory exceeds vm.dirty_background_ratio (10% of RAM); above vm.dirty_ratio (20%) writers are throttled (latency stall).
  • Durability: a successful write() does not mean the data is on disk. fsync(fd) forces data (and metadata) out and waits; fdatasync skips some metadata. Databases call fsync on commit, hence the cost of WAL (about 0.1 ms on NVMe, 5 to 10 ms on HDD). O_DIRECT bypasses the cache (Oracle, some Postgres/MySQL modes manage their own buffer pool).
free -m
#               total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
# Mem:          15984  6120   310     210        9553       9400
grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback|Cached' /proc/meminfo
# Cached:  9100000 kB   Dirty: 1204 kB   Writeback: 0 kB
echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches     # only for testing! (drops cache)
vmtouch -v /data/file.db              # how much of a file is cached (tool)
fincore file.db                       # util-linux equivalent
iostat -x 1                           # r/s w/s await %util on the device

Production incidents.

  • Latency spikes every ~30 s on a write-heavy box: big dirty flushes saturate disk and throttle writers; lower dirty_background_bytes so flushing starts earlier and in smaller chunks.
  • After restart a database is slow for minutes: cold cache; warm up with a scan or pg_prewarm.
  • A backup or cp of a huge file evicts hot data; use nocache, posix_fadvise(DONTNEED) or O_DIRECT.
  • Power loss loses writes that were not fsynced; a filesystem or app that lies about durability corrupts data (famous Postgres "fsyncgate" 2018 showed fsync error handling was subtler than assumed).

Industry examples. Kafka deliberately relies on the OS page cache for both writes and reads (it keeps little JVM heap, so caching is not duplicated and survives broker restarts); Elasticsearch advises leaving at least half of RAM for the page cache; Postgres uses its own shared_buffers plus the page cache (double buffering).

Decision gravity. Relying on the OS cache is simple and reversible; managing your own buffer pool (O_DIRECT) gives control and predictable behaviour but you take on cache logic and double-caching risks; a one-way door at database-architecture level.

Everyday analogy. A librarian keeps recently requested books on the front desk; returning requests are instant, and when the desk is full the least recent go back to the stacks.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading "free memory is 300 MB" as a problem. Look at available.
  • Believing write() returning means data is durable.
  • Forgetting that the page cache is counted in a container's memory cgroup, and can contribute to hitting memory.max (it is reclaimable, but confuses dashboards).

notes.title: Memory troubleshooting checklist
notes.html:
A practical flow when "the server is out of memory" or "memory keeps growing".

  1. System view: free -m, vmstat 1, cat /proc/meminfo, cat /proc/pressure/memory.
  2. Who holds it: ps aux --sort=-rss | head, smem -rtk (PSS), pmap -x <pid>.
  3. Swap activity: vmstat si/so, per-process VmSwap.
  4. Kernel memory: slabtop, /proc/meminfo Slab, PageTables.
  5. Kills: dmesg -T | grep -i oom, container memory.events, kubectl describe pod.
  6. Is it growth or burst? Graph RSS, working set, page cache and major faults over days.
  7. Native vs managed: JVM -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory; Android dumpsys meminfo <pkg> and Android Studio profiler.
$ ps aux --sort=-rss | head -3
USER  PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ     RSS TTY  STAT START TIME COMMAND
app  4410 85.0 61.2 9123456 9983212 ?   Sl   Nov07 122:11 java -jar svc.jar
$ cat /proc/pressure/memory
some avg10=2.31 avg60=1.20 avg300=0.40 total=1234567
full avg10=0.55 avg60=0.20 avg300=0.05 total=345678

Rule of thumb for sizing a JVM container limit of 4 GiB: heap 2.5 GiB, leaving about 1.5 GiB for metaspace (~100 to 300 MB), thread stacks (200 threads x 1 MB), code cache (~240 MB), direct buffers and the allocator overhead.

Everyday analogy. A household budget check: total money, who spends the most, whether there is a debt (swap), and whether a bill collector (OOM killer) has come.

Common interview traps.

  • Only looking at the heap dump for a native leak.
  • Restarting the service and calling it fixed without capturing dmesg, RSS history and a heap or native profile first.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Programs get memory from allocators (glibc, jemalloc, tcmalloc) that grow via brk/mmap; frames arrive on first touch.
  • Allocators keep size-class bins, coalesce neighbours and use per-thread caches; MALLOC_ARENA_MAX or jemalloc often fix RSS creep.
  • Internal fragmentation is waste inside blocks, external is unusable holes; Linux uses buddy and slab allocators; Redis shows mem_fragmentation_ratio.
  • Swap holds cold anonymous pages; watch si/so activity, tune swappiness, consider zram; latency-critical services minimise it.
  • Overcommit plus the OOM killer: oom_score, oom_score_adj, cgroup limits, exit code 137, read dmesg and memory.events; size JVM heaps below container limits.
  • mmap maps files into memory with lazy loading and sharing but brings page-fault latency and SIGBUS risks.
  • The page cache absorbs file I/O: readahead, dirty write-back, fsync for durability, available not free; Kafka and Elasticsearch lean on it.
  • Triage: system view, top RSS, swap, kernel memory, kill logs, managed vs native.

questions.promptHtml: What happens when you call malloc(100) or new, and what does free really do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks the layered model (allocator, then kernel, then physical frames) that underlies every memory debugging session.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: malloc is a library function, not a syscall. The allocator (glibc, jemalloc, tcmalloc) serves the request from free blocks it already holds. Only when it has none does it ask the kernel to grow the heap with brk or map fresh memory with mmap; large requests (glibc default threshold 128 KB, dynamic) go straight to mmap. Neither syscall commits RAM: frames arrive on first touch via page faults. free usually just returns the block to the allocator's free list, not to the OS.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
your code -> malloc/new -> allocator free lists -> (brk | mmap) -> kernel -> frames on first touch
$ strace -e trace=brk,mmap,munmap ./app
brk(0x55e1c8a5d000) = 0x55e1c8a5d000          # heap grew 132 KB
mmap(NULL, 1048576, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0) = 0x7f2c...

Consequences:

  • A process's RSS can stay high after it frees most of its objects, because the allocator keeps pages for reuse (and holes in the heap prevent brk from shrinking).
  • Big blocks (mmaped) are returned with munmap on free, so they do shrink RSS.
  • new byte[100MB] in Java advances a pointer in a heap the JVM reserved at start; the first write to each 4 KB page costs a minor fault (25,600 here), so -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch moves that cost to startup.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying malloc is a syscall.
  • Expecting RSS to drop after free.
  • Confusing the JVM garbage collector with the native allocator underneath.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is malloc(1GB) fast? -> It only creates a mapping; frames are allocated on touch.
  2. What does malloc_trim(0) do? -> Asks glibc to return free heap pages to the OS.
  3. How does free know the size? -> A header just before the block records it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "allocates heap memory". Senior describes the allocator layer, brk vs mmap, lazy commit, why RSS stays high, and the choice of jemalloc/tcmalloc.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service's RSS never fell after traffic dropped and was reported as a leak; it was glibc retaining freed pages, solved by jemalloc and arena limits.

questions.subtopic: free vs available and page cache
questions.promptHtml: free -m shows only 300 MB free on a 16 GB server. Is the server out of memory? What is the page cache?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A very common misreading; the answer reveals whether you understand Linux memory accounting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Not necessarily. Linux uses otherwise idle RAM as page cache, keeping recently read and written file data so most file I/O never touches disk, and gives it back under pressure. free is the wrong column; I look at available, an estimate of what can be allocated without swapping. If available is 9 GB, the box is fine.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
$ free -m
        total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:    15984  6120   310     210        9553       9400

Behaviour:

  • Read: first read misses and fills the cache (about 100 microseconds on NVMe); later reads come from RAM (under a microsecond).
  • Readahead prefetches sequential data (default 128 KB).
  • Writes land as dirty pages; flusher threads write them back after dirty_expire_centisecs (30 s) or when dirty exceeds dirty_background_ratio (10% of RAM); above dirty_ratio (20%) writers are throttled.
  • A successful write() is not durable; fsync makes it so.

Real pressure signals: available low, sustained si/so in vmstat, PSI memory, kswapd CPU, OOM in dmesg.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Alerting on free memory.
  • Running echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches "to free memory" in cron; it throws away useful cache.
  • Forgetting that in containers the cache counts toward the cgroup memory.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you see what is cached? -> fincore, vmtouch, /proc/meminfo Cached.
  2. What makes a database slow after restart? -> Cold cache; warm with pg_prewarm or a scan.
  3. Does cache count as used in Kubernetes? -> Working-set includes active cache; reclaimable but can confuse dashboards.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "free is cache, don't worry". Senior explains available, writeback thresholds, readahead, fsync semantics, cgroup accounting, and what true pressure looks like.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An alert on free memory paged a team nightly for a healthy Kafka broker whose job was to fill RAM with log segments.

questions.promptHtml: What is swap, when is it useful, and why do many latency-critical services still avoid it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests nuance beyond "swap is bad".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Swap is disk space that holds anonymous memory pages evicted from RAM; clean file-backed pages never need swap, they are dropped and re-read. It is useful because it lets the kernel push cold pages (an idle daemon's heap) out so RAM serves the hot working set and cache, and it cushions short spikes. Latency-critical services avoid it because a swapped-in page is a major fault costing 0.1 to 10 ms, and a swapping JVM stalls GC badly. The signal of trouble is active swap traffic (si/so), not the amount of swap used.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
pressure ladder: free RAM drops -> drop clean cache -> compress (zram/zswap) -> swap to disk -> OOM killer

Tuning: vm.swappiness (default 60, databases often 1-10) is a preference between swapping anonymous pages and dropping cache, not an on/off switch. zram/zswap compress pages in RAM (about 2-3x) and are default on many laptops and phones. Kubernetes historically required swap off; newer versions allow limited node swap (verify for your version).

swapon --show
vmstat 1                                         # si/so KB/s
grep -E 'SwapTotal|SwapFree' /proc/meminfo
grep VmSwap /proc/<pid>/status                   # who is swapped

Worked example: a 16 GB host with a 10 GB database and 8 GB of mostly idle daemons: 4 GB swap lets the kernel park 3 GB of cold heap, leaving the DB cache intact; without swap the DB's cache shrinks first.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Swap off is always best".
  • Concluding there is a problem from used swap alone; check traffic.
  • Believing swappiness=0 disables swap.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does continuous si/so mean? -> Working set exceeds RAM: thrashing.
  2. Why zram on phones? -> Avoids flash wear and is faster than flash.
  3. Why not swap for JVM heaps? -> GC touches the whole heap, forcing pages in and out.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "slow, avoid". Senior: it helps by evicting cold pages, measure traffic not usage, use zram, set per-workload policy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A database host with swap off lost its page cache first during a spike and got slower than the same host with 2 GB of swap that parked cold daemon pages.

questions.contextHtml:
A Spring Boot service in Kubernetes (limit 4 GiB, request 4 GiB, -Xmx3g) restarts every 6-8 hours. Heap dashboards show 1.8 to 2.4 GB used, never near 3 GB, and no OutOfMemoryError in logs.

$ kubectl describe pod payments-5c7 | grep -A3 'Last State'
    Last State: Terminated   Reason: OOMKilled   Exit Code: 137
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events
oom_kill 3
$ jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary | grep -E 'committed' | head
Java Heap: committed=3145728KB   Thread: 410 threads committed=420000KB
Class: committed=250000KB   Code: committed=240000KB
Internal/Other (direct buffers): committed=620000KB

Total committed is about 4.7 GB. A teammate proposes raising -Xmx to 3.5g "so it has more room" and another suspects a heap leak.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the pod being OOM killed and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases heap or hunts a heap leak although the heap never filled; ignores native memory.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What counts toward the cgroup limit (RSS plus page cache)? Is there a MaxDirectMemorySize set? Is thread count growing? What is the latest deploy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the container limit to 6 GiB (headroom) while lowering heap, or roll back the last change; this stops restarts so we can investigate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) container limit smaller than heap plus off-heap (the JVM budget is over-committed by design: 3 GB heap + 0.25 metaspace + 0.24 code + 0.42 stacks + 0.62 direct); (b) direct buffer or native leak (Netty); (c) thread leak; (d) page cache accounting.
  4. How I'd verify: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary over time (enable -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary); compare container working set vs heap; cat memory.stat; thread count over time.
  5. Root cause: The kernel kills the container when the total (heap committed 3 GB + metaspace + code cache + 410 thread stacks at 1 MB + 620 MB direct buffers + allocator overhead) crosses 4 GiB, long before the heap itself is full. The JVM does not know about the cgroup limit relative to the sum of all its pools; heap dashboards show only one slice. Raising -Xmx makes it worse.
  6. Fix: Reduce heap to about 60-70% of the limit (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65), cap direct memory (-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m), limit threads, and size the limit from the NMT budget. If direct memory keeps growing, find the leak (unreleased Netty buffers; -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=advanced).
JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65 -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"
  1. Prevention: Alert on container working-set / limit > 85%; memory budget table per service; restart reason dashboards (OOMKilled count).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lower heap means more GC pressure (watch GC time). I would not raise Xmx or only restart on a schedule. A rule of thumb: for a 4 GiB limit start with a 2.5 GiB heap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How is it different from a Java OutOfMemoryError? -> That is the JVM refusing allocation within its own limits; the OOM killer is the kernel with SIGKILL, so no stack trace.
  • Does the page cache count? -> Yes, but it is reclaimable, so it rarely causes the kill itself.
  • Why did it take 6 hours? -> Direct buffers and threads grew slowly with traffic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Every restart looked like random flakiness until the team compared the sum of NMT pools to the limit: the configuration had been over-committed since day one and only crashed when traffic filled the pools.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raises Xmx or hunts a heap leak.
  • Hire: Accounts for off-heap memory, sets heap to a fraction of the limit.
  • Strong hire: Uses NMT, caps direct memory, adds working-set alerts, distinguishes kernel OOM from Java OOM.

questions.promptHtml: How does a general-purpose allocator like glibc malloc or jemalloc work internally, and why do multithreaded servers care which one they use?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes understanding of size classes, coalescing and per-thread caching, which explain real fragmentation and RSS-growth incidents.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The allocator carves large chunks from the kernel into blocks with a small size header. Free blocks sit in bins by size class; freed neighbours coalesce into larger blocks. To avoid a global lock on every call, each thread has a cache or arena (tcache in glibc, thread caches in tcmalloc/jemalloc), trading some memory for speed. For long-running multithreaded servers, jemalloc and tcmalloc usually show less fragmentation and lock contention than glibc, and switching is as simple as LD_PRELOAD.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
[hdr|used 32][hdr|FREE 64][hdr|used 16][hdr|FREE 128]
free(2nd) next to a free neighbour -> coalesce into one bigger block

Policies from textbooks (first, best, worst fit) are replaced in practice by segregated fits: size classes (roughly power-of-two steps) give O(1) allocation at the cost of internal waste (33 bytes served from a 48-byte class).

Allocation path: thread cache hit returns immediately; miss goes to an arena's bins (taking its lock); empty bins grow with brk or mmap.

glibc creates up to 8 x cores arenas, and each retains freed memory; a service with many threads may show RSS creep. Levers: MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2, malloc_trim, jemalloc with background_thread and decay settings.

MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 ./app
LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/libjemalloc.so.2 ./app

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing up JVM GC with the native allocator.
  • Forgetting thread caches hold memory per thread.
  • Assuming a custom allocator is always faster; measure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is internal waste in size classes? -> The rounding gap between request and class; typically about 10-25% depending on class spacing.
  2. Why coalesce? -> To rebuild large blocks and reduce external fragmentation.
  3. How do you profile allocations? -> jemalloc prof, tcmalloc heap profiler, heaptrack, perf on malloc.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "free list". Senior covers size classes, coalescing, arenas/caches, the memory-for-speed trade, and concrete tuning knobs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Switching a C++ service from glibc to jemalloc dropped steady RSS by roughly 30% in one fleet (verify per workload).

questions.contextHtml:
A Python/C++ hybrid ingestion service (gunicorn plus a native extension, 64 threads in a pool, 16-core node) has steadily growing memory: 1.2 GB after deploy, 3.9 GB after 4 days, and then it is OOM-killed (limit 4 GB). Python object counts (tracemalloc, gc) are flat. The native extension's own allocation counter says 120 MB live.

$ pmap -x <pid> | awk '$3 > 20000' | head
00007f2c40000000  65404  65320  65320 rw---   [ anon ]
00007f2c44000000  65412  64900  64900 rw---   [ anon ]
...  (about 40 anonymous ~64 MB regions)
$ cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep Threads
Threads: 66

Leak checkers (valgrind on a short run) show nothing. The next step proposed is "rewrite the extension".
questions.promptHtml: What is the likely cause and how do you confirm and fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Insists on a leak and a rewrite, though live counters are small; does not recognise the 64 MB arena pattern.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: glibc version? Do threads allocate in one thread and free in another? Does RSS shrink when idle? Is MALLOC_ARENA_MAX set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 (or 4) in the service environment, and schedule rolling restarts before 3.5 GB to avoid kills while confirming.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) glibc per-thread arenas, each retaining freed memory and fragmented (the 64 MB [anon] regions at 7f2c4*000000 are the signature); (b) a true leak; (c) Python arena fragmentation; (d) memory-mapped file growth.
  4. How I'd verify: malloc_stats() or malloc_info (via gdb: call malloc_info(0, stdout)) lists arenas with free bytes; check live vs RSS gap (120 MB live, GBs RSS); try LD_PRELOAD jemalloc and compare RSS after one day; malloc_trim(0) called from gdb to see how much returns.
  5. Root cause: With many threads glibc creates up to 8 x cores = 128 arenas, each an independent 64 MB heap. Freed memory in an arena stays there, mixed with live blocks, so it is not returned to the OS and cannot be used by other arenas. RSS tracks the fragmented high-water mark of every arena, not live data, so it grows even though nothing is leaked.
  6. Fix: Short term: MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2, optionally MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_. Long term: jemalloc with decay-based purging (MALLOC_CONF=background_thread:true,dirty_decay_ms:5000), reduce pool size to cores, reuse buffers in the extension.
export MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2
# or
LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libjemalloc.so.2 MALLOC_CONF=background_thread:true gunicorn app:app
  1. Prevention: Track RSS minus live-bytes ratio; soak test of 24 hours before release; document allocator settings in the runbook; add memory to the alerting dashboard.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Fewer arenas increases lock contention (measure throughput; tcache mitigates it). jemalloc has its own tuning and its profile differs. I would not rewrite the extension before proving a real leak.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How to prove it is not a leak? -> Live-bytes counter flat, malloc_info shows large free totals, RSS plateaus with fewer arenas.
  • Why does it grow more with more threads? -> More arenas, each with its own retained free memory.
  • Does free return memory to the OS? -> Only when trimming the top of a heap, or for mmaped chunks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent weeks hunting a leak in a C extension. Setting one environment variable flattened the graph and was found by someone who counted the 64 MB mappings in pmap.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Assumes leak and proposes a rewrite.
  • Hire: Recognises arena fragmentation and applies MALLOC_ARENA_MAX or jemalloc.
  • Strong hire: Proves it with malloc_info/pmap, discusses contention trade-offs and soak testing.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Linux memory overcommit modes and how the OOM killer chooses a victim. How does this differ inside a container?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: OOM events are among the most common production memory incidents; the answer shows operational depth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: By default (vm.overcommit_memory=0) Linux lets processes allocate more virtual memory than exists, betting most will never touch it all; only absurd requests are refused. Mode 1 always allows (Redis recommends it so fork does not fail); mode 2 is strict and fails allocations up front. If physical memory runs out, the OOM killer scores processes by memory use adjusted by oom_score_adj and sends SIGKILL to the highest. In a container, hitting the cgroup memory.max triggers an OOM kill inside that cgroup even when the host has free RAM; Kubernetes reports OOMKilled, exit 137.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Scoring: roughly proportional to the process's share of memory; /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj ranges from -1000 (never kill) to +1000 (kill first). Kubelet sets adjustments by QoS class: Guaranteed pods protected, BestEffort first.
  • Strict mode 2: limit = swap + ratio x RAM; failures show up as clean ENOMEM but waste capacity and break fork-heavy programs.
  • Evidence:
$ dmesg -T | grep -i -A3 'out of memory'
Out of memory: Killed process 4410 (java) total-vm:9123456kB, anon-rss:7654320kB ... oom_score_adj:0
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<grp>/memory.events
oom_kill 2
  • Userspace policies exist: Facebook's oomd uses PSI to kill by policy before the kernel does; Android's lmkd kills background apps.
# Container OOM
Container allocates -> Reaches memory.max -> Reclaim fails -> OOM killer SIGKILL -> Exit 137 -> Restart

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing the OOM killer kills the last allocator; it kills by score.
  • Debugging an OOMKilled pod by looking only at the heap; native memory counts.
  • Setting oom_score_adj=-1000 on a leaking process and letting the kernel kill something critical instead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Redis suggest overcommit=1? -> fork for BGSAVE can look like it doubles memory; heuristic mode may refuse it.
  2. Can you catch the OOM kill? -> No, SIGKILL is uncatchable; you only see it afterwards in dmesg/events.
  3. Node-level vs cgroup OOM? -> Node OOM is global and picks across processes; cgroup OOM stays inside the limited group.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "kills processes when out of memory". Senior knows the modes, scoring and adjust values, cgroup vs global, how to read the evidence, and sizing limits versus memory pools.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A node-level OOM killed the node agent instead of the leaking batch job because the agent had a larger RSS and default score; lowering its score and limiting the job fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A write-heavy ingestion node (32 GB RAM, NVMe) shows p99 write latency flat at 4 ms, then every ~30 seconds a spike to 800 ms for 2-3 seconds. CPU is idle during spikes. The application appends to files via write() and never calls fsync.

$ while sleep 1; do grep -E '^(Dirty|Writeback):' /proc/meminfo | tr '\n' ' '; echo; done
Dirty: 410000 kB  Writeback: 0 kB
Dirty: 3150000 kB Writeback: 0 kB
Dirty: 6400000 kB Writeback: 980000 kB     <- spike here
Dirty: 900000 kB  Writeback: 2400000 kB
$ sysctl vm.dirty_ratio vm.dirty_background_ratio vm.dirty_expire_centisecs
vm.dirty_ratio = 20
vm.dirty_background_ratio = 10
vm.dirty_expire_centisecs = 3000
$ iostat -x 1   -> nvme0n1 wkB/s 1.9 GB/s, %util 100 during spikes

Someone proposes faster disks; someone else wants to call fsync after every write.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the periodic spikes and how you would fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Buys faster disks or adds per-write fsync (which would make things slower), without understanding write-back thresholds.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is durability required (what is acceptable loss on power cut)? Average write rate? Does the latency hit all writers? Any recent RAM increase?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower the thresholds so write-back starts earlier in smaller chunks: set vm.dirty_background_bytes=256MB and vm.dirty_bytes=1GB. Live change, no restart.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) large accumulated dirty data (up to 10% of 32 GB = 3.2 GB) flushed in a burst that saturates the disk, throttling writers past dirty_ratio; (b) fsync from another process; (c) GC pause; (d) noisy neighbours on the disk. The Dirty graph sawtooth plus %util 100 fits (a).
  4. How I'd verify: Sample Dirty/Writeback every second as above; iostat -x; perf trace-like checks for balance_dirty_pages stalls (offcputime/bcc if available); apply the sysctl and see if the sawtooth flattens.
  5. Root cause: write() only copies into the page cache and returns fast. Dirty pages accumulate until the background threshold; then the flusher writes them in bulk. If dirty data keeps growing past dirty_ratio, the kernel makes the writing processes themselves wait in balance_dirty_pages. With big RAM, percentage-based thresholds mean gigabytes of dirty data, so one flush takes seconds.
  6. Fix: Short term: byte-based thresholds as above. Long term: if durability matters, batch and fdatasync at group-commit intervals on the application side, smooth the write rate, or use sync_file_range to flush incrementally.
sysctl -w vm.dirty_background_bytes=268435456   # 256 MB
sysctl -w vm.dirty_bytes=1073741824             # 1 GB
  1. Prevention: Dashboard on Dirty/Writeback and write-latency percentiles; a sysctl baseline for write-heavy hosts; load tests on production-sized RAM.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lower thresholds reduce write coalescing and increase disk IOPS slightly. Per-write fsync costs 0.1 ms on NVMe and 5-10 ms on HDD and kills throughput. I would not disable the cache (O_DIRECT) without a buffer strategy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does this lose data on power failure? -> Yes, anything not fsynced; thresholds shorten the exposure only a little.
  • Why is dirty_bytes better than ratio? -> Ratio scales with RAM, so a 512 GB box can hold 50 GB dirty.
  • What if the spikes remain? -> Disk may truly be saturated; check device queue depth and burst limits of cloud volumes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A logging pipeline had a 'mysterious 30-second heartbeat' of timeouts. The 30 seconds was exactly dirty_expire_centisecs; byte-based thresholds made it vanish.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Faster disks or fsync per write.
  • Hire: Explains dirty write-back and tunes thresholds.
  • Strong hire: Byte-based limits, group commit for durability, verification with Dirty/Writeback sampling, discusses trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
A Redis primary on a 32 GB instance is at 90% memory and the team wants to double the instance size ($$). INFO memory:

used_memory:            10737418240     (10.0 GB)
used_memory_rss:        17179869184     (16.0 GB)
mem_fragmentation_ratio:1.60
mem_allocator:          jemalloc-5.2.1
active_defrag_running:  0
maxmemory:              0

The workload has many keys with varying value sizes and heavy expiry/deletes. A replica on an identical instance has used_memory 10.0 GB and RSS 11.2 GB. Another engineer says "RSS 16 GB means we really use 16 GB; we need 64 GB nodes."
questions.promptHtml: Explain the gap, propose the cheapest fix, and what you would monitor.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Doubles the instance, or declares the ratio meaningless.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the ratio steady or growing? Is it ever below 1 (swapping)? How much memory does the replica show after a fresh sync? Fork/BGSAVE behavior and latency tolerance?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set maxmemory (with an eviction policy appropriate to the use case) so growth is bounded; enable activedefrag yes with conservative CPU limits.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) external fragmentation from variable-size allocations plus deletes (RSS/used = 1.6); (b) memory held for COW during BGSAVE; (c) output buffers/client buffers; (d) swap (ruled out as ratio > 1).
  4. How I'd verify: The replica with identical data at 1.12 shows the data fit in about 11 GB and the primary's problem is layout, not data; MEMORY DOCTOR, INFO memory, MEMORY STATS, allocator stats MEMORY MALLOC-STATS; check active_defrag metrics after enabling.
  5. Root cause: Over time, free holes between live objects can't be reused by differently sized new allocations, and allocator pages with a few live objects cannot be returned to the OS. About 6 GB of RSS is waste, not data.
  6. Fix: Enable active defrag (activedefrag yes, active-defrag-cycle-min 5, max 25) and watch CPU and latency; the cheaper operational trick is to fail over to the freshly synced replica and rebuild the old primary, which resets fragmentation; then keep defrag on. Bounded maxmemory avoids nodes running to the edge.
CONFIG SET activedefrag yes
CONFIG SET active-defrag-cycle-min 5
CONFIG SET active-defrag-cycle-max 25
  1. Prevention: Alert on mem_fragmentation_ratio above 1.5 for hours and below 1.0 (swap); track RSS versus used_memory per node; plan capacity on used_memory plus a 20-30% headroom for fragmentation and fork.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Active defrag consumes CPU and can add latency; start low. Failover has a brief blip and needs sync completion. I'd not double the instance for a layout problem, and I'd not treat ratio < 1 as good: it means Redis memory is partially swapped.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is the replica's ratio lower? -> It loaded data compactly during sync, with no history of churn.
  • Can MEMORY PURGE help? -> It asks jemalloc to release dirty pages, which can return some, but defrag/failover addresses layout.
  • When is 64 GB right? -> If used_memory plus BGSAVE COW headroom truly approaches the limit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cache fleet's bills dropped by a third after enabling active defrag and rotating primaries monthly; the 'growth' was fragmentation, not data.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Doubles instance size.
  • Hire: Reads the ratio, enables defrag or failover to reset.
  • Strong hire: Compares replica to isolate layout, sets maxmemory and alerts on ratio both ways, discusses CPU/latency trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: When is mmap better than read/write for file I/O, and what are its hidden costs and failure modes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many engineers assume mmap is "faster"; interviewers want trade-offs, especially for databases and search engines.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: mmap maps file pages into the address space so I access them as memory; the kernel loads pages lazily through page faults and the page cache page is mapped directly, avoiding the copy that read does into a user buffer. It shines for random access to large files, sharing one cached copy across many processes, and simple code. Costs: page faults replace explicit I/O so latency is unpredictable (a cold miss is a major fault), I/O errors arrive as SIGBUS rather than error codes, TLB shootdowns on unmap, and write-back timing is out of my control (msync). For sequential streaming, read with large buffers is about as fast.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Flavours: file-backed MAP_SHARED (writes go to the page cache and back to the file, visible to other mappers), file-backed MAP_PRIVATE (copy-on-write; how executables and libraries load), and anonymous (big mallocs, thread stacks).

import mmap
with open("data.bin", "r+b") as f:
    m = mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0)
    print(m[0:16])        # faults pages in lazily
    m[0:4] = b"ABCD"      # dirties a page
    m.flush()             # msync
touch address -> page fault -> kernel reads page into page cache -> maps it -> instruction retried

Worked example: searching a 50 GB index with 20 processes: with read and private caches it could need 1 TB; with mmap all share 50 GB of page cache.

Why some databases moved away from mmap (the CMU paper "Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your DBMS?"): lack of control over eviction and flush ordering (breaks write-ahead logging guarantees), I/O stalls on page faults blocking threads, error handling via SIGBUS, and scalability limits from page-table and TLB contention.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "mmap is always faster".
  • Not handling SIGBUS when the file is truncated by someone else under a mapping.
  • Assuming a store through the mapping is durable; it needs msync (and fsync semantics).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Lucene use it? -> MMapDirectory for index files, relying on the OS cache; leave RAM free for page cache.
  2. Why does Kafka use sendfile for reads? -> Zero-copy from page cache to the socket without a user-space copy.
  3. How do you prefetch mapped data? -> madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) or MAP_POPULATE.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "faster, no copying". Senior weighs random vs sequential access, page-fault latency, SIGBUS, WAL ordering, shootdowns, and knows when explicit buffer pools win.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search cluster had p99 spikes after deploy because the new nodes' mapped index pages were cold; pre-touching the files with vmtouch fixed warm-up.

questions.contextHtml:
A small order-ingest service writes each accepted order to a journal file, acks the client, and replays the journal on restart. After a host power loss, 4 seconds of acknowledged orders were missing and the last record was half-written. The code:

import os, json

class Journal:
    def __init__(self, path):
        self.f = open(path, "ab")

    def append(self, order):
        data = (json.dumps(order) + "\n").encode()
        self.f.write(data)          # buffered Python file object
        self.f.flush()
        return True                  # caller acks the client now

    def rotate(self, new_path):
        os.rename(self.f.name, new_path)
        self.f = open(self.f.name, "ab")

The disk is an NVMe SSD; the filesystem is ext4 with default options; the team says "flush() writes it to disk".
questions.promptHtml: Identify every durability bug and describe the correct design, including cost.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "flush() should be enough" or "use a database" without explaining what flush does and where data sits.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What loss is acceptable (RPO)? Order rate (affects fsync batching)? Is the disk's write cache power-protected? Do clients need the ack to imply durability?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop acknowledging before sync; add os.fsync and reconcile missing orders from upstream/client retries.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) flush() only moves data from Python's buffer into the kernel page cache; it is still lost on power failure; (b) rotation/rename not synced (directory entry not durable); (c) torn last record, no checksums; (d) device write cache lies.
  4. How I'd verify: strace -e trace=write,fsync,fdatasync shows write but no fsync; grep Dirty /proc/meminfo shows unflushed data; reproduce with a crash test (VM power cut or dm-flakey/CrashMonkey-style tool).
  5. Root cause: write() and flush() copy bytes into the page cache; the kernel writes them back after about 30 s or at the dirty thresholds. The ack was sent before the data was on stable storage, so a power loss dropped the cached tail and left a partial record. The fsync step was missing entirely, and a new file or rename needs the directory synced too.
  6. Fix: fsync (or fdatasync) before ack; batch concurrent appends into a group commit; add length-prefix plus CRC per record so replay stops at the first torn record; fsync the directory after creating or renaming.
def append_batch(self, orders):
    buf = b"".join(frame(o) for o in orders)   # len + crc32 + payload
    os.write(self.fd, buf)
    os.fdatasync(self.fd)                       # durable before ack
    return True

def rotate(self, new_path):
    os.fsync(self.fd); os.rename(self.path, new_path)
    dfd = os.open(os.path.dirname(new_path) or ".", os.O_DIRECTORY)
    os.fsync(dfd); os.close(dfd)
  1. Prevention: Crash-recovery tests in CI (kill -9 and power-cut simulation), checksum validation on replay, durability stated in the API contract, monitoring of fsync latency.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: An fsync costs about 0.1 ms on NVMe (5-10 ms on HDD); group commit amortises it at the price of a small latency wait. Not O_SYNC for every tiny write unless the rate is low. Not trusting a consumer-grade SSD without power-loss protection. Lower dirty_expire is not a substitute.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if fsync fails (EIO)? -> Treat as fatal; retrying fsync on the same pages may report success while data is lost (the Postgres "fsyncgate" lesson, 2018).
  • fdatasync vs fsync? -> fdatasync skips non-essential metadata, but file size changes are still synced.
  • Does a kernel crash lose the page cache? -> Yes, same as power loss.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue 'never lost data' in testing and lost minutes in its first datacentre power event; the fix was twelve lines (fdatasync, CRC, directory fsync) and a crash test that ran on every merge.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Believes flush() is durable.
  • Hire: Explains page cache vs disk, adds fsync before ack.
  • Strong hire: Group commit, CRC for torn writes, directory fsync, fsync-failure semantics, and cost numbers.

questions.contextHtml:
Every night at 02:00 a nightly backup (cp of a 400 GB database directory to a network volume) runs on the primary of a 128 GB-RAM PostgreSQL server. Between 02:00 and about 05:30 query latency rises 8x, and the morning dashboards are slow until about 08:00. Evidence:

$ free -m   (01:55)
Mem: 128000  45000  900  4100  82000  80000
$ free -m   (03:00)
Mem: 128000  45500  1100  4100  81400  79000     <- cache size the same!
$ pg_buffercache / pg stats: shared_buffers hit ratio  99.7% -> 94%
$ vmtouch -v /pgdata/base/16384 | tail -2     (03:00)
  Resident Pages: 5100000/48000000   (~10% of hot DB files cached; was ~70%)
$ iostat -x 1  -> nvme0n1 r/s 21000, await 1.9 ms

The team says "cache is the same size so it can't be a cache problem" and wants to add RAM.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the slowdown and how you'd fix the backup without a hardware change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds RAM; concludes the cache is fine because the total buff/cache is unchanged.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the backup read the same files Postgres serves from? Is shared_buffers a fixed 32 GB? Could the backup run on a replica? Is it a file-level copy or pg_basebackup?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause (SIGSTOP) the backup when latency alerts fire, or re-run with nocache/ionice; rate-limit it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the backup streams 400 GB through the page cache, evicting the database's hot pages and replacing them with once-read backup data; (b) I/O contention on the disk (but await 1.9 ms is fine); (c) network volume congestion; (d) vacuum running at the same time.
  4. How I'd verify: vmtouch hot-file residency before and after (70% to 10%); the same total buff/cache is the clue: the cache is full but of the wrong contents; fincore of the backup source files; run the backup with posix_fadvise(DONTNEED) and compare residency.
  5. Root cause: The page cache is a global LRU-like structure, and a one-pass read of 400 GB looks, to the replacement policy, like very recently used data, pushing out genuinely hot pages. Queries then miss in cache and hit disk (hit ratio 99.7% to 94% means 20x more misses). It recovers only as queries slowly re-warm the cache, hence latency stays high until 08:00. Total size unchanged hides the churn.
  6. Fix: Short term: run the copy through nocache cp, dd iflag=direct, or rsync with --drop-cache/posix_fadvise; ionice -c3; throttle bandwidth. Long term: take the backup from a replica or a snapshot (LVM/EBS snapshot), use pg_basebackup from a standby, and optionally restrict the job's cache with a memory cgroup (memory.high) so its cache cannot take over the host.
ionice -c3 nice -n19 nocache rsync --bwlimit=200m -a /pgdata/ backup:/vol/
# or let the job drop what it reads:
dd if=file iflag=direct of=/backup/file bs=8M
  1. Prevention: Alert on cache residency of hot files and on hit ratio; run backups on replicas; include backup in capacity tests; schedule outside peaks.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: O_DIRECT reads skip readahead and cache so the backup is slower (acceptable); memory.high limits slow the job. Not adding RAM, since any size is flushed by a large enough scan. Not drop_caches after the backup, which throws away the entire hot set.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does shared_buffers not save you? -> Postgres relies on the OS cache for double-buffering; hits that missed shared_buffers were served from the OS cache and are now disk reads.
  • Would MGLRU help? -> Newer kernels resist scan pollution better (verify behaviour on your kernel), but do not rely on it.
  • Why were reads fast (1.9 ms await) yet queries slow? -> Many more random reads per query, adding up.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "mysterious" daily brownout ended when the backup moved to a standby; nobody had noticed the page cache turning over completely every night.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds RAM; says cache unchanged means fine.
  • Hire: Identifies scan pollution and uses nocache/fadvise or throttling.
  • Strong hire: Proves with hot-file residency, moves backup to replica/snapshot, uses cgroup limits, and avoids drop_caches.

questions.contextHtml: You run a fleet of 200 Kubernetes nodes (64 GB) with swap disabled (the historical default). Pods are a mix: latency-sensitive APIs (Guaranteed QoS), Burstable batch workers, and many idle sidecars and JVM services that sit at 30% of requested memory. Finance wants better bin-packing (denser nodes). Last quarter, OOM kills hit mostly bursty batch pods during spikes, costing retries. A proposal on the table: enable swap on all nodes (e.g., 16 GB zram or NVMe swap, swappiness=60). SRE worries swap will cause latency regressions for APIs.
questions.promptHtml: Do you enable swap? Design the policy and the rollout, and say what evidence would change your mind.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Swap is bad, never" or "yes, enable everywhere" with no isolation, measurement or rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Kubernetes version and whether node swap with per-pod controls is supported (verify); disk type (NVMe vs network); are API pods Guaranteed; what do PSI and si/so look like now; is the OOM cost mostly retries or SLO breaches?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No fleet-wide change. Start with a canary pool of 10 nodes dedicated to batch/burstable workloads while APIs stay on the no-swap pool.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) swap helps by parking cold pages of idle sidecars, freeing RAM for hot work and absorbing batch spikes; (b) swap hurts APIs if their pages get evicted (major faults at 0.1-10 ms); (c) compressed swap (zram) gives most of the benefit at lower tail cost but spends CPU and RAM; (d) the OOM kills are caused by wrong limits, which swap would hide.
  4. How I'd verify: Canary metrics: OOM kill count, p99 of colocated APIs, major faults, si/so, PSI memory some/full, node CPU for zram, pod restart rate; A/B against the control pool for two weeks including a peak; check kernel/Kubelet behaviour for Burstable-only swap (NodeSwap with LimitedSwap; verify availability).
  5. Root cause (of the dilemma): Denser packing relies on idle memory being reclaimable. Cold anonymous pages can only be reclaimed with swap; without it the only reclaim is page cache, so the kernel's first lever is OOM. But swap converts memory shortage from a crash into slowness, which is worse for latency tiers.
  6. Fix (policy): Enable swap only on batch/general pools (zram first with small size, or NVMe swap), set swappiness moderate, keep API pools swap-free or with swap restricted so Guaranteed pods don't use it; set memory requests/limits correctly; use PSI-based eviction (oomd/kubelet) to evict early instead of thrashing; roll out per pool with canary and automatic rollback.
  7. Prevention: SLOs on PSI full and si/so on swap-enabled nodes; policy as code for pool labels; dashboards that attribute swap by pod; regular review of requests vs actual usage so swap is not a crutch.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Swap can mask leaks and make failures slow instead of loud; zram steals CPU and RAM; NVMe swap wears SSDs. I'd not enable on API nodes or mix tiers on the same swap-enabled node, and I'd not use swap as a substitute for right-sizing. Evidence that would change my mind: if canary shows APIs unaffected and OOM kills halved I'd extend; if major faults on Guaranteed pods rise, I'd roll back.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the disk is network-attached? -> Swap latency becomes unpredictable; prefer zram or avoid.
  • How do you stop swap thrash? -> PSI-driven early eviction and per-cgroup memory.swap.max.
  • Hibernate-style use? -> Unrelated; this is about cold-page offload.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A platform team enabled zram on batch nodes only, saw OOM kills drop by 70% with no API impact, and then discovered half of their 'needed' memory requests were two years stale.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Absolute yes/no, no measurement plan.
  • Hire: Tiered decision with canary and metrics.
  • Strong hire: Pool-level policy, zram vs disk, PSI-based eviction, per-cgroup swap limits, explicit rollback criteria.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review of a recurring problem: a Go-and-Java platform node has had "memory alerts" for three weeks. The on-call's usual response was to restart the biggest process. Yesterday the node OOM-killed its logging agent and the database sidecar, causing data gaps. Facts from the timeline:

RSS of 'ingest' process:  Nov 1: 1.1 GB   Nov 8: 2.9 GB   Nov 15: 5.8 GB (restart)  
$ dmesg -T | grep -i oom    (Nov 15, after the restart notes were lost)
Out of memory: Killed process 2211 (fluent-bit) total-vm:... anon-rss:380MB
Out of memory: Killed process 3098 (pgsidecar) ... anon-rss:910MB
$ cat /proc/meminfo | grep -E 'Slab|PageTables|SUnreclaim'
Slab: 9100000 kB   SUnreclaim: 8800000 kB   PageTables: 140000 kB
$ slabtop -o | head -4
 OBJS ACTIVE USE OBJ SIZE SLABS
 41000000 40900000 99% 192 bytes   dentry

The ticket history says "restarted ingest, memory back to normal" six times with no data captured.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: what are the real problems, what did the team miss, and what's the corrected triage process?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart earlier / add RAM / ingest leaks"; no structure and no attention to kernel memory or evidence capture.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does ingest create and delete many files (tmp files, sockets)? Is the 5.8 GB RSS heap or native? What is available before the kills? Are there cgroup limits? What other process was biggest at kill time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop reclaimable slab as a stopgap only to restore headroom (echo 2 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches) while capturing evidence first; protect critical agents with oom_score_adj and memory reservation; restart ingest only after capturing a heap/native profile.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) two separate problems: ingest RSS growth (a leak or retention) and a kernel slab explosion (8.8 GB dentry objects, largely from negative dentries created by looking up many nonexistent file names); (b) page cache; (c) fragmentation; (d) a scheduling problem where critical agents had default OOM scores.
  4. How I'd verify: For ingest, jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info / VM.native_memory or Go pprof heap and GODEBUG memory stats; RSS vs heap gap tells native vs managed; for slab, slabtop, /proc/slabinfo, perf or strace -c on file-lookup syscalls, identify which process stats thousands of missing paths; check oom_score ordering and MemAvailable history.
  5. Root cause: The review's root cause is process, not just a leak: six restarts masked a trend and destroyed evidence (no RSS history, no profile, dmesg lost). Technically there were two independent consumers of 15 GB: ingest growth over weeks (~1 GB/week at first, then faster) and kernel slab (unreclaimable here) at 8.8 GB. Together they pushed MemAvailable to zero, and the OOM killer chose by score, picking the lightweight but unprotected agents.
  6. Fix: Short term: capture heap/native profile on the next growth cycle, find and fix the lookups creating negative dentries (e.g., probing for nonexistent files per request, or a cache directory of random names), cap with periodic cleanup, and set oom_score_adj negative for critical agents with memory limits on ingest. Long term: a memory runbook following the checklist.
Triage: free -m / vmstat 1 / /proc/meminfo / PSI  ->  top RSS (ps --sort=-rss, smem PSS)
        -> swap activity -> kernel memory (slabtop, PageTables) -> kill logs (dmesg, memory.events)
        -> growth or burst? (graphs over days) -> managed vs native (NMT, pprof) -> fix and watch
  1. Prevention: Retain per-process RSS, available, slab and PSI history for 30+ days; alert on trend (slope) not threshold; pre-restart capture script; memory.max on workloads and MemoryLow protection for agents; ban "restart and close" without an attached artifact.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: drop_caches is a diagnostic crutch (it hurts performance); the ratio of reclaimable vs unreclaimable slab matters. I would not simply scale RAM, and not tune vfs_cache_pressure before learning what produces the dentries.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is dentry growth possible on a healthy box? -> Negative dentries cache failed lookups; a workload probing unique missing names grows them without bound until pressure.
  • How would you tell JVM from native growth? -> RSS far above committed heap suggests native; confirm with NMT summary.
  • What if memory growth is a burst rather than trend? -> Look at queue depth, large payloads and per-connection buffers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Six identical 'restart fixed it' tickets hid a daily growth slope; the first time anyone graphed RSS over 30 days it was a straight line with a clear cause in a retry cache.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Keeps restarting; adds RAM.
  • Hire: Follows a structured triage, spots kernel slab as a separate cause, protects critical processes.
  • Strong hire: Separates technical and process root causes, mandates evidence capture, trend alerting and managed vs native diagnosis.
